title: Student GIS Portfolio
text:
This portfolio presents selected GIS, cartography, research, volunteer, and professional-development work completed while I was a student. Most of the projects come from the GIS Certificate program at Roane State Community College and my graduate studies at the University of New Mexico, with additional context from my first GIS courses at Tennessee Tech University.
I reconstructed this portfolio from files preserved on old hard drives, archived presentations, reports, maps, and material from a now-defunct personal website. It is intended to show students how coursework and early professional experiences can be documented in a portfolio—even when the path into a career is not direct.
Explore the Projects Read My Learning Path

title: Student GIS Portfolio
text:
A Nonlinear Path into GIS
My path into GIS was neither direct nor carefully planned. I first encountered GIS as an undergraduate at Tennessee Tech, but initially pursued graduate study and a career in education. Several years later, I returned to the subject by enrolling full-time in the GIS Certificate program at Roane State Community College while working and attending classes at night.
I began that transition in fall 2008, just as the Great Recession was affecting employment throughout the geospatial industry. Although entering the field took longer than expected, coursework, volunteer GIS projects, conferences, professional organizations, and new relationships helped me continue developing both technical skills and confidence.
Graduate study at the University of New Mexico added advanced coursework, funded research assistantships, independent thesis research, conference presentations, and applied work supporting statewide geospatial programs. Over time, experiences that once seemed disconnected—including education, GIS, research, outreach, and professional service—came together to support a career drawing on all of them.
The projects in this portfolio document that progression: from learning individual GIS tools to designing independent projects, conducting research, communicating results, serving professional communities, and applying geospatial skills to real problems.

title: Student GIS Portfolio
text:
Featured Student Projects
These projects represent several stages of my development as a GIS student. Each began in a different context, but together they demonstrate how classroom assignments, independent research, volunteer work, and funded projects can become meaningful portfolio examples.


Camp Davy Crockett Asset Inventory
Roane State Community College
An independent field-based project involving geodatabase design, domains and subtypes, GPS data collection, asset photography, data processing, and maps created for both camp management and visitors.
View project →


Arches National Park
Roane State Community College
A collaborative geodatabase project combining two-dimensional and three-dimensional visualization, demographics, elevation, fire hazard, trails, streams, recreation, and wildlife habitat analysis.
View project →


GIS Thesis
University of New Mexico
An example of the complete graduate research process, including literature development, proposal design, spatial methods, analysis, interpretation, and presentation of findings.
View project →


Haiti Earthquake Data Comparison
University of New Mexico
A comparison of asserted and authoritative geospatial data associated with the January 2010 Haiti earthquake, emphasizing data quality and emergency decision-making.
View project →


Predictive Crime Mapping
University of New Mexico
Funded graduate research examining predictive crime-mapping methods and the robustness of kernel-density hotspot maps, later presented at regional GIS conferences.
View project →


American Red Cross Shelter Accessibility
Volunteer GIS Project
An applied volunteer project mapping emergency shelter locations and examining potential geographic gaps in shelter coverage.
View project →

Mars SPIRIT Rover Traverse Map
text:
This map was my first substantial cartographic project using ArcMap. I completed it as an individual project in GIS 105: Computer Cartography at Roane State Community College during fall 2008.
The poster follows the traverse of NASA’s SPIRIT rover across the surface of Mars within Gusev Crater. It combines maps at several scales, moving from the rover’s location on Mars to a detailed view of the landing site, rover path, and associated spacecraft components.



Complete Mars SPIRIT Rover traverse poster.

section: Exploring the Map at Multiple Scales
text:
Exploring the Map at Multiple Scales
The poster used a sequence of locator and detail maps to help readers move from the entire planet to the immediate landing area.






Small-scale locator map showing the location of Gusev Crater relative to the entire surface of Mars.







Regional locator map showing Gusev Crater in relation to Elysium Mons and Ma’adim Vallis.











Enlarged view of Gusev Crater showing the SPIRIT rover traverse.







Detailed landing-site map showing the lander, backshell, parachute, and heat-shield impact locations.

section: From Class Project to Conference Submission
text:
From Class Project to Conference Submission
My instructor and advisor, Pat Wurth, encouraged students to attend professional GIS events and submit work to conference map galleries. Following her recommendation, I entered this poster in the map gallery at the November 2008 Northeast Tennessee GIS User Group Conference in Kingsport, Tennessee.
This was the first map I submitted at a GIS conference. Attending the meeting allowed me to see professional and student GIS work, reconnect with one of my earlier GIS professors, meet people working in the field, and begin participating in Tennessee’s professional GIS community.



Standing beside the Mars SPIRIT Rover poster at the 2008 Northeast Tennessee GIS User Group Conference.

title: Mars SPIRIT Rover Traverse Map
text:
What I Learned
This project taught me several lessons that extended beyond the finished poster:

GIS data may use a local coordinate origin that must be reconciled with the map’s coordinate system.
Spreadsheet calculations can support GIS data preparation and coordinate adjustment.
Locator maps at multiple scales can help readers understand an unfamiliar geographic setting.
A course project can become a professional-development opportunity when it is shared beyond the classroom.
Presenting work publicly helped me begin building confidence as a member of the GIS community.

title: Mars SPIRIT Rover Traverse Map
text:
Looking Back
This map reflects my skills, the available software, and common cartographic practices at an early point in my GIS education. Some design choices are different from those I would make today, but I have preserved the original poster rather than redesigning it.
Its value lies not only in the finished map, but also in what it represents: an early technical challenge, my first substantial ArcMap project, and my first experience sharing student GIS work at a professional conference.
